scope.description: Hand-researched deepening pass for Japanese Hanada City Gym / Misty and four cards that carry the deck's collector logic.
in_scope: Hanada City Gym / Misty release dossier
not_claiming: official copy counts beyond cited deck quantities

context.name_ja: ハナダシティジム カスミ

sources.title: Local Japanese pre-English release catalog: Hanada City Gym / Misty
PokéCardex series page: Hanada City Gym

claims.text: The local catalog, PokéCardex, and Bulbapedia all place Hanada City Gym / Misty on April 26, 1998.

Bulbapedia describes Hanada City Gym as a Japanese-exclusive Standard Deck that complements Leaders' Stadium, while the local catalog models the product as a gym standard deck with 24 unique card rows.
Bulbapedia says the deck contains 64 fixed cards rather than the usual 60; the local catalog and PokéCardex expose 24 unique non-Energy rows for the deck-family catalog surface.

Bulbapedia says most cards in the deck were not found in the Japanese main expansion and that those cards were added to the main set for English release; it also says the deck contents provided the basis for the English Misty Theme Deck.
Bulbapedia calls Misty's Goldeen and Misty's Tentacool two notorious Gym Heroes 'common rares' and ties that English rarity memory to their fixed rarity in this Japanese deck.

The local catalog's attention rows for Hanada City Gym / Misty include Misty's Psyduck, Misty's Poliwag, Misty's Tentacool, Misty's Tentacruel, Misty's Seel, Misty's Goldeen, Misty's Starmie, and Misty's Tears.
The local catalog's credited-artist clusters for Hanada City Gym / Misty are Ken Sugimori, Keiji Kinebuchi, and Atsuko Nishida.

Hanada City Gym / Misty matters because it is a fixed-deck character object that later becomes English set texture: the deck's private distribution logic, no-rarity deck context, common-rare memory, and Misty-specific card choices all travel differently when the cards are reassembled for English Gym-era collecting.

not_claiming: row-level symbol proof from a seller image
steps: Confirm the card belongs to the Hanada City Gym / Misty deck family, not the 1996 Expansion Pack No Rarity family.
Treat the deck-family no-rarity symbol status as release context, not as proof that a seller's physical card has been inspected.
For English Gym Heroes/Gym Challenge comparisons, check whether the card was reassembled into an English expansion or theme-deck context before importing rarity assumptions.
When a card name overlaps a later English Gym card, preserve the Japanese deck row identity and cite the local row id.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Hanada City Gym cards can be missing rarity symbols because they are fixed-deck Japanese Gym cards; that must not be laundered into a 1996 No Rarity Base Set claim.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing Hanada City Gym / Misty cards, especially when a seller uses 'no rarity' language.

narrative.human_title: Misty as a deck, not just a character
narrative.why_it_matters: Hanada City Gym is where a Gym Leader becomes a small machine: 64 fixed cards, water lines, trainer personality, and a few rows that later look strange in English binders. This is exactly the kind of release an agent has to understand historically, because the same card-shaped object can mean fixed-deck memory in Japan, set rarity weirdness in English, and seller shorthand in a marketplace listing.

sources.title: Local Hanada City Gym row: Misty's Psyduck 001
Bulbapedia deck list: Hanada City Gym

claims.text: The local catalog identifies Misty's Psyduck as Hanada City Gym / Misty row 001.
The local catalog credits Misty's Psyduck to Atsuko Nishida.
Bulbapedia's Hanada City Gym deck list shows Misty's Psyduck as a single-copy Pokémon row in the fixed deck.
Misty's Psyduck is the front door to the deck's personality: a single-copy row by Atsuko Nishida that lets the binder feel like Misty rather than simply Water type.

not_claiming: all Misty's Psyduck prints share the same source context
steps: Confirm the release family is Hanada City Gym / Misty and preserve row 001.
Do not collapse this row into later English Gym-era Misty's Psyduck records without an explicit print/context match.
Use the local artist credit as catalog metadata, not as physical-card authentication.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Misty's Psyduck should be treated as a specific Hanada City Gym row before an agent compares it to other Misty-era Psyduck cards.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A buyer or seller identifies a card as Misty's Psyduck from the Japanese Misty deck.

narrative.human_title: The little row that makes it Misty
narrative.why_it_matters: A deck can be mathematically Water type and still feel anonymous. Misty's Psyduck keeps that from happening. It is one copy, early in the row order, and credited to Atsuko Nishida; the card works like a character signature before the deck settles into its water engine.

sources.title: Local Hanada City Gym row: Misty's Tentacool 003
Bulbapedia: Hanada City Gym common-rare note

claims.text: The local catalog identifies Misty's Tentacool as Hanada City Gym / Misty row 003.
The local catalog credits Misty's Tentacool to Ken Sugimori.
Bulbapedia names Misty's Tentacool as one of the notorious Gym Heroes 'common rares' created by the card's fixed-rarity origin in the Japanese Hanada City Gym deck.
Misty's Tentacool is a useful agent test because its importance is not the character alone; the row carries a rarity-translation story from fixed Japanese deck card to English common-rare memory.

not_claiming: English rarity applies to the Japanese deck row
steps: Confirm whether the listing is for Japanese Hanada City Gym row 003 or an English Gym Heroes/Gym Challenge-era card.
If a seller says 'rare' or 'common rare,' ask which release context they mean before treating the word as a price or scarcity claim.
Preserve the Japanese fixed-deck origin separately from English set rarity language.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Misty's Tentacool is a rarity-language trap: fixed-deck Japanese context and English common-rare memory should remain separate.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing or agent note uses rarity language for Misty's Tentacool.

narrative.human_title: A tiny card with a rarity afterlife
narrative.why_it_matters: Misty's Tentacool is not a chase because Tentacool suddenly became Charizard. It is interesting because the card remembers how products were assembled. A fixed-deck Japanese row becomes a strange English rarity story, and that is exactly the kind of context a good agent should keep from flattening.

sources.title: Local Hanada City Gym row: Misty's Goldeen 009
Local Hanada City Gym row: Misty's Goldeen 010
Bulbapedia: Hanada City Gym common-rare note

claims.text: The local catalog identifies Misty's Goldeen row 009 and Misty's Goldeen row 010 as separate Hanada City Gym / Misty rows.
The local catalog credits row 009 to Atsuko Nishida and row 010 to Ken Sugimori, making the duplicate species name an artist-sensitive distinction.
Bulbapedia names Misty's Goldeen as one of the notorious Gym Heroes 'common rares' created by the card's fixed-rarity origin in the Japanese Hanada City Gym deck.

Misty's Goldeen is a cataloging pressure point: two same-name deck rows, two artist credits in the local catalog, and later English rarity memory mean an agent should ask which row is being discussed before sounding confident.

steps: Ask whether the card is Hanada City Gym row 009 or row 010 before importing artist or image context.
Use the image/reference row only as catalog comparison, not as proof of a seller's physical card.
Keep English common-rare language separate from the Japanese fixed-deck row identity.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Misty's Goldeen has duplicate same-name row pressure; row identity matters before artist, image, or rarity language can be trusted.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing or user note says Misty's Goldeen without a row number or image.

narrative.why_it_matters: Misty's Goldeen is a perfect small-card lesson. It looks like something you could wave away as filler, but the deck gives you two same-name rows and the catalog gives them different artist traces. That is the whole Cairn problem in miniature: the row matters before the story can be honest.

sources.title: Local Hanada City Gym row: Misty's Tears 018
Bulbapedia deck list: Hanada City Gym

claims.text: The local catalog identifies Misty's Tears as Hanada City Gym / Misty row 018.
Bulbapedia gives the Japanese title as カスミのなみだ, rendered Kasumi's Tears.
The local catalog credits Misty's Tears to Ken Sugimori, and Bulbapedia's gallery labels both English and Japanese prints as illustrated by Ken Sugimori.
Bulbapedia says Misty's Tears is one of several cards whose artwork changed between Japanese and English releases.
Bulbapedia's card text says Misty's Tears discards one other card from the player's hand to search the deck for up to two Energy cards.
Misty's Tears is the deck's clearest variant-boundary card: it links Japanese deck origin, English Gym Challenge naming, Ken Sugimori credit, and artwork-change memory in one row.

not_claiming: English and Japanese artwork are interchangeable
artwork comparison alone proves a physical card
steps: Preserve the Japanese title カスミのなみだ / Kasumi no Namida when explaining the Hanada City Gym row.
Do not compare a seller image only against the English Gym Challenge artwork; this card has a documented Japanese/English artwork-change boundary.
Confirm the release context before treating the card as Hanada City Gym, Gym Challenge, or another print.
Use artwork match as a reference clue only; require seller evidence before any transaction claim.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Misty's Tears needs variant-aware comparison because the Japanese and English artwork histories diverge.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A buyer, seller, or agent uses Misty's Tears imagery, English Gym Challenge references, or Japanese deck references interchangeably.

narrative.human_title: The card where comparison can lie
narrative.why_it_matters: Misty's Tears is exactly why this catalog cannot be a flat checklist. The name, art credit, deck origin, English set memory, and artwork-change boundary all pull on the same object. An agent that knows this card should not sound more certain; it should ask a better question.
